items.title: Planetary VC founder @ramez reveals that throwing 100 Claude Opus 5.5 agents at a problem was no bet...
items.content:
Planetary VC founder @ramez reveals that throwing 100 Claude Opus 5.5 agents at a problem was no better than using just 10, exposing a major limitation of AI swarms:

"Test time compute scales worse than pre-training. Agents scale worse than test time compute. On the Opus 5.5 model card, it is like the worst scaling we've ever seen of anything."

"The success of one agent was like 70%. It gained three points when you went to four agents, and then it gained two points when you went from four agents to 16. The Opus 5.5 model just topped out after 10 agents. It didn't get any better with 100 agents."

"If you took the population of Columbus, Ohio, and said, 'Create general relativity,' would they do as well as Einstein on his own? There are many categories of problems where the peak intelligence of one entity is much more important than having a lot of entities at a lower level collaborating."

items.content:
Planetary VC founder @ramez explains why the AI intelligence explosion may be much further away than people think, with the current feedback loop still 5–10x too weak to sustain itself:

"The thing that has never made full sense about the FOOM story to me is this feedback loop: a better AI makes better algorithms, better chips, and that leads to an even better AI. But most problems are much harder than linear, so you have diminishing returns."

"OpenAI very proudly said researchers are using 124 times more tokens per person. We're getting 7 times more lines of code per person. And we're getting 1.6 times as many experiments per person."

"When you plug that data into the formal models of a FOOM, the current feedback loop is about a factor of 5 to 10 too weak to sustain itself, even if there were no humans in the loop."

items.content:
I'd frame it as follows: The data industry has taken off in recent years, but the quality of our net output is still far too low (amplifying behaviors like reward hacking). 

We're working to build scalable methods for creating sample-efficient data for RL. In order to keep this pipeline going, we need to push the frontier of evaluation science, while building specific benchmarks to hillclimb on areas of clear economic value.

I've been advising Mercor on how to build this research direction effectively. These are my views, but I'm confident we're going to see a major investment from economy around the frontier labs (open inference, open post-training, and data) orient around expertise in building real-world representative evals and synthetic data methods to scaling training data around them.

I’m personally very excited about this, it is the research that will make more of the economy “feel the AGI” for the first time.
(And, there’s a big opportunity to build this on open models.)

Planetary VC founder @ramez argues that Dario Amodei's warnings about an imminent AI intelligence explosion don't match Anthropic's own system cards:

"The statements from Dario, the statements from the top of OpenAI about how close they are don't look like their data or even like their system cards."

"Anthropic's is actually really good. If AI can increase the pace of AI development by a factor of two, that's the dangerous level. Every system card they've put out has said, 'Nope, we're not there.'"

"In the Mythos system card, they said, 'We think it would have to improve the productivity of our team members by a factor of 40 to double the rate of AI progress, and we think right now it's improving productivity by a factor of four.'"

"Ideas get harder to find. Right now some of the AI gains are just being soaked up by helping us maintain the current pace of progress."

Recently had the chance to interview @benhylak on how he is thinking about simulations in our AI Evals Course 😁

Simulations are incredibly useful for evals when you do them well. Ben discusses what he learned from implementing simulations for evals at several companies. Some fun topics came up, my favorite being "simulation awareness" - when models know they are in a simulation.

Below is a chapter summary:

 Why input/output tests miss agent failures
 Replay production traces to see what a change breaks
 Recreate the data and tools around the agent
 How agents detect simulations and change their behavior
 Choose scenarios that test the change you made
 Check answers, costs, and tool behavior across runs
 Replay known failures to verify a fix
 Common mistakes that make simulations misleading
 Check that the simulation reproduces production behavior
 When to start using simulations

You can also watch this on YT: https://t.co/JOCncyIMH9

It still has gaps in cinematic fidelity, complex motion and dense scenes, and full scale training is still underway. Real time works through the API today, and browser tools are coming.

I want to see those gaps close while the price stays this low.

Planetary VC founder @ramez explains why AI's enormous appetite for training data could become a major limitation, with Waymo needing 10 million miles to learn what teenagers can in under 1,000:

"If you have to get training data by attempting things on humans, that means your data is much more limited. And current AI models require an enormous amount more training data than we do."

"A teenager gets their driver's license after less than 1,000 miles of driving. It took Waymo the first 10 million miles on real roads and a few billion in simulators to get to human-level skill."

"We will eventually solve this. I'm not a carbon chauvinist. We will eventually make true general superintelligence."

"But the models we have right now are gonna rock in places where there is an epic amount of training data, and in the places where it's more sparse, I think they might remain very imperfect."

"a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful" 

This feels like the next evolution of SEO/AEO that every product will try to game. Even if agents do the equivalent of ~10 hours of research on a product, it's less important on whether the product is actually better vs. the agent's perception that the product is better.

Agents might do deep research on evals and benchmarks; yet anyone who's worked on evals knows that it's hard to create a truly unbiased one that can universally measure product quality. They might optimize for human preferences, in which case companies will optimize for user reviews and feedback. 

Companies will optimize for whatever preferences the top AI models have been posttrained on.

LineShine: China's Exascale Supercomputer Advances High Performance Scientific Computing! The World's Fastest Speed: World Record. 

LineShine-supercomputer, developed by the Shenzhen Cloud Computing Center and deployed at the National Supercomputing Center in Shenzhen (NSCS), has emerged as a major contender in high performance computing. It is the first system to eclipse 2 exaflops using a CPU only design. It circumvents traditional CPU-GPU heterogeneous setups by embedding AI matrix acceleration units directly into the processor itself.

The system achieved 2.198 exaflop/s on the High Performance LINPACK (HPL) benchmark, the world’s fastest speed, utilizing 13,789,440 processing cores and exceeding the performance of the ranked system by more than 20%, exceeding 2 quintillion calculations per second.

Built around China's independently developed computing architecture, LineShine incorporates 300-core LX2 processors operating at 1.55 GHz, a proprietary LingQi high-speed interconnect, and the Kylin operating system.

Beyond traditional floating-point performance, LineShine demonstrated exceptional computational efficiency across additional benchmarks:

* HPCG: Achieved 22 petaflop/s, securing first place in the High Performance Conjugate Gradients benchmark.  These chips operate at a frequency of 1.55 GHz and utilize the ArmV9 instruction set architecture
* HPL-MxP: Recorded 7.92 exaflop/s in mixed-precision computing, and representing approximately 3.6 times its HPL performance.

These measurements highlight the system's ability to handle computationally intensive scientific workloads while relying on a CPU-only architecture.

Researchers in Shenzhen also submitted results for consideration for the prestigious Gordon Bell Prize, which recognizes major advances in computational science and supercomputing.

Beyond its technical achievements, LineShine represents an important development in China's international supercomputing, Addison Snell of Intersect360 Research observed that the more unexpected development was not China's ability to construct a world-leading supercomputer, but its renewed interest in obtaining formal recognition through international rankings.

From custom multicore processors and high-speed interconnects to exascale scientific calculation, LineShine demonstrates the growing importance of indigenous computing architectures in advancing high-performance computing and AI-driven scientific discovery.

* HPCG: Achieved 22 petaflop/s, securing first place in the High Performance Conjugate Gradients benchmark. These chips operate at a frequency of 1.55 GHz and utilize the ArmV9 instruction set architecture

* HPL-MxP: Recorded 7.92 exaflop/s in mixed-precision computing, and representing approximately 3.6 times its HPL performance.

These measurements highlight the system's ability to handle computationally intensive scientific workloads while relying on a CPU-only architecture.

Researchers in Shenzhen also submitted results for consideration for the prestigious Gordon Bell Prize, which recognizes major advances in computational science and supercomputing.

items.content:
💾 Two years ago I started working on these crazy nostalgia projects, kind of randomly, because I was bored and wanted to do something different than just build another SaaS or AI app/website

I wanted to try to run Windows 3.1 inside a web browser, and to do that properly already took me months

When that worked well enough, I wanted to build a dial up internet connection so it could browse the web, with the basic levels of AI back then, that was VERY hard, and I'd just go around in circles forever. Finally I had to find the only person in the world who got that working @bai0 and beg him to help me make it work, and we did it!

Then I started hosting classic games like Quake with full multiplayer, porting them to WASM, or if not already like Quake III by @lukathedev and hosting those with a full multiplayer server ready-to-go in your browser

And then I spent 6 months trying to reverse engineer Windows XP to run on v86 by @copy_sh, very difficult (because it's so big) and only possible because modern AI like  Opus 5.5 is good enough to figure that out

For the last two years pretty much nobody cared about any of these projects, I'd tweet them into the void, which was fine because I thought it was very fun just for myself

But now with this wave of AI-assisted reverse engineering WASM ports of games and apps to web they're finally taking off, pretty much anything is portable to WASM on web now, and if you add server to it via WebSockets, people can instantly play with each other, or interact inside apps you host, it's super cool

Every game and app I have on @pieter now is full or almost full to the limit, yesterday 80,000 people played around in Windows 3.1 or Windows XP inside their browsers chatting to MSN and AOL Messenger AI bots and playing 3D Pinball or playing Quake etc.

And that was my idea for @pieter: a non-commercial preservation project, kinda like an online computer museum but interactive!

The most cool thing to pay respects to these old games, apps and OSes I think is to keep them alive by making them easily and freely accessible, playable on mobile so old and new generations of people can jump back in the past interactively

This is one of my first projects to take off that does not, can not and will not make money because it's non-profit, and that's fine

Every time I tweeted about these projects would always ask me "but why?" 

Because it's really fun! 🤩

That's what I mean by SEARCH. 
Though there are way more efficient ways to perform search than generation-selection of discrete token sequences.

Some LLMs do search when they produce multiple outputs (auto-regressively) in silence and then evaluate them and select the best one. 
The overall process is not auto-regressive token prediction.

GRE 2026–2027 — What Scores Do You Need for Graduate Computer Science at America's Top Universities?

Master the GRE! Target Stanford, MIT, Carnegie Mellon, Berkeley, Princeton, and Georgia Tech!

Graduate admissions in Computer Science, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Data Science are highly competitive, but here's an important development in 2026: Many of America's top Computer Science universities no longer require the GRE! They’re waiving!

Top U.S. Universities — GRE Requirements for Graduate Computer Science (MS/PhD)

• Stanford University: GRE NOT required or considered — MS/PhD Computer Science.

• MIT: GRE NOT required — EECS graduate admissions, except the special LGO pathway.

• UC Berkeley: GRE NOT required or accepted — EECS research graduate programs.

• Carnegie Mellon University (CMU): Depends on the program. GRE required for MS in Artificial Intelligence and Innovation and Master of Computational Data Science.

• Princeton University: GRE Not Required — Computer Science graduate programs.

• Harvard University: GRE Optional — Computer Science PhD.

• Cornell University: GRE Not Reviewed — CS MS; GRE has no admission impact for CS MEng.

• University of Washington: GRE Not considered — Computer Science PhD.

• Georgia Tech: GRE OPTIONAL — MS Computer Science.

• UIUC: GRE Not required — MS Computer Science.

• UCLA: GRE Optional under its published 2025–2026 CS admissions policy;

• UC San Diego: GRE Not required — MS/PhD Computer Science for Fall 2027.

• UT Austin: GRE Optional — Computer Science graduate programs.

• Purdue University: GRE Not required — CS graduate programs.

• University of Maryland: GRE Not required — CS graduate admissions.

Universities Publishing Numerical GRE Benchmarks

• University of Illinois Chicago (UIC): International MS CS applicants generally require GRE Quantitative + Verbal ≥300, including Verbal ≥140, subject to exemptions.

University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC): GRE Not Required for MS, MCS, Online MCS, or PhD Computer Science! GRE scores may be submitted optionally—recommended undergraduate GPA: 3.2 for master's programs and 3.4 for PhD admission.

• University of Illinois Springfield (UIS): GRE Not Required for MS Computer Science, including on-campus program! Minimum undergraduate GPA: 2.70 The 32-credit-hour program covers software development, algorithms, programming, and computer science foundations. Fall, Spring, and Summer admission available, with international on-campus admissions limited to Fall and Spring.

• Columbia University — CS MS Bridge: GRE Optional. Previously reported admitted-student averages: Quantitative 161, Verbal 159, Analytical Writing 4.0. These are historical averages, NOT minimum admission requirements.

What Is a Competitive GRE Score for Computer Science?

• 330–340: Exceptionally strong overall score
• 325–329: Very competitive overall score
• 320–324: Strong overall score
• 310–319: Competitive for some programs
• 300–309: May satisfy some published minimums

These are general preparation benchmarks, not university-issued specific admission cutoffs. For quantitative CS programs, a high GRE Quantitative score can be particularly valuable where the GRE is considered.

What Matters Beyond the GRE?

• GPA and undergraduate academic performance
• Data Structures, Algorithms, and Discrete Mathematics
• Linear Algebra, Probability, and Statistics 
• Python, C++, Java, and software development
• Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning project
• Research experience and publications
• Statement of Purpose and Letters of Recommendation
• Faculty research alignment for PhD applicant
Important: GRE NOT required does not mean admission is easier! At universities that do not consider GRE scores, strong academic records, technical experience, research accomplishments, and peer recommendations become even more important. If you’re looking for a recommendation, contact me!

A 330+ GRE score does NOT guarantee admission to Stanford, MIT, CMU, or Berkeley — and at universities that do not consider GRE scores, even a perfect 340 provides no direct admission advantage!

A strong GPA, Computer Science foundations, research experience, programming skills, recommendation letters, and statement of purpose can matter significantly more than GRE performance.

An Infinite Descent into Pure Mathematics by Clive Newstead (2022) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks.

This textbook is designed for students transitioning from computational, problem-solving mathematics—such as standard calculus—into abstract pure mathematics and rigorous proof construction.

This textbook is designed for students transitioning from computational, problem-solving mathematics—such as standard calculus—into abstract pure mathematics and rigorous proof construction.

It assumes minimal technical prerequisites beyond elementary algebra and familiarity with standard number systems, though occasional exercises draw on basic calculus techniques.

Rather than training students to execute mechanical algorithms, the book aims to convert passive consumers of mathematical formulas into active producers of rigorous arguments, establishing the foundational concepts and reasoning habits required for advanced study in pure mathematics.

Quantum Computing for the Quantum Curious by Hughes et al. (2021) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks.

It's an introductory textbook designed to bridge the gap between popular science expositions and advanced undergraduate courses.

Aimed at high school students, early undergraduates, and scientifically literate general readers, the text assumes only a background in basic wave concepts from introductory high school physics.

Computer programming experience is not required, and appendices provide reviews of essential probability, statistics, and linear algebra concepts such as vectors and matrices.

Structured for roughly fifteen to twenty hours of study, the textbook introduces the core principles of quantum information science—superposition, measurement, and entanglement—without attempting to serve as a comprehensive survey of modern physics.
